title: Robust Topologically Protected Edge Transport in Doubly Chiral Active Particles
authors: Tristan Edwards, Maxim Nikolaev, Jaime Agudo-Canalejo
abstract: Using theory, simulation, and experiment, we introduce a new class of active particle which we term doubly chiral active Brownian particles (dcABPs), which show robust topologically protected transport along boundaries without backscattering at corners. Their double chirality stems from the coexistence of an intrinsic angular velocity, which can cause rotation independently of translation, and a translation-rotation coupling inducing cross-alignment to the instantaneous velocity, which causes rotation only concomitantly with translation. A mechanically detailed model shows that the latter effect can arise from an asymmetric friction distribution in the direction perpendicular to the self-propulsion direction. We show that topologically protected modes emerge when the two sources of chirality have opposite sign and the intrinsic rotation is weaker than the translation-rotation coupling. In the deterministic limit, we characterize the emergence of these modes not only along straight boundaries, but also along curved boundaries and during interparticle interactions. We provide a proof-of-principle experimental realization by building a doubly chiral vibrobot. While setting the work into context, we moreover show that the topologically protected boundary-induced transport of dcABPs stands in contrast to the edge currents observed for simple chiral ABPs, which we demonstrate are not associated with boundary-induced transport, as well as to those observed for chiral active rods or self-aligning chiral ABPs, which we show to be associated with boundary-induced transport but to backscatter at corners, implying lack of topological protection.
summary: This paper introduces doubly chiral active particles (dcABPs) that exhibit a unique form of topologically protected transport along boundaries. By rigorously contrasting this behavior with simpler models, the authors establish a new physical mechanism for directed motion in active matter. The work bridges theoretical derivation, simulation, and experimental realization using vibrobots.
main_problem: To determine the conditions under which robust, topologically protected boundary-induced transport can occur in active particles, contrasting this with edge currents observed in simpler chiral models.
main_result: Doubly chiral active Brownian Particles (dcABPs) exhibit robustly protected directed motion along boundaries, unlike simple cABPs or chiral rods which either lack protection or backscatter at corners.
method: The work combines theoretical analysis of steady-state probability currents with detailed numerical simulations and the design/testing of a physical vibrobot realization.
model_or_system: The primary model is the doubly chiral active Brownian particle (dcABP), characterized by two sources of chirality: an intrinsic angular velocity and a translation-rotation coupling arising from asymmetric friction. The analysis extends to simple cABPs and chiral rods in confined geometries (channels, arenas).
key_observables: Edge currents ($J_y(x)$ or $J_\phi(r)$), integrated net transport ($\Phi$), and the persistence of directed motion around corners.
important_parameters: The relative strengths of intrinsic rotation versus translation-rotation coupling, and the presence/absence of boundary curvature are critical parameters determining topological protection.
main_assumptions: Initial analyses often assume overdamped dynamics for cABPs; later work rigorously derives transport using stochastic averaging techniques applicable to various noise regimes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematics comparing current distributions and cumulative displacement for different particle types (cABP vs. dcABP) in confined geometries, demonstrating the failure of simple models to achieve true boundary-induced transport.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes that simple cABPs do not exhibit true boundary-induced transport ($\Phi$ arises from bulk orbits). It then contrasts this with chiral rods showing backscattering. Finally, it introduces and proves the topological protection mechanism for dcABPs using theory (Appendix A) and simulation/experimentation.
why_interesting: While focused on classical active matter, the concept of 'topological protection' in non-equilibrium systems is highly relevant to understanding robust edge states in quantum materials or engineered quantum circuits where dissipation and noise are present.
